**Candidates** (from `candidate_specs.md`):
- **Sensor-T1:** thin-pitch sensor with large signal sharing.
- **Sensor-T3:** planar sensor with standard pitch.
- **Sensor-T2:** 3D-electrode sensor with larger pitch.

**Thickness ranges:** The documents give no per-technology ranges. Only the global 50–300 µm limit applies.

**Resolution:** The only numbers are from the 2025 simulation, which was unirradiated and at 150 µm:

| Sensor | Single-hit resolution |
|---|---|
| T1 | 6.0 µm |
| T3 | 9.0 µm |
| T2 | 14.0 µm |

**Other facts:**
- The readout chip supports 50×50 µm² pixels and a 1.5 GHz/cm² hit rate, and all three candidates are compatible with it.
- Cooling is CO2 evaporative at -35 °C.
- Power is 7 W per module.

**Missing from the documents:** I found no data on trapping, bias, threshold or material budget.

**Open issue:** `simulate_resolution` only covers unirradiated sensors. So the efficiency requirement will have to be handled by physics reasoning or flagged as unverified. One line of reasoning is that trapping limits thick planar sensors, while 3D sensors are radiation hard. I did not run any simulations in this step.

I recorded all of this with `record_results`.

None has efficiency, charge-collection, trapping, depletion or bias, or threshold data, and none gives per-technology thickness ranges. I did not call `simulate_resolution`, because it only covers unirradiated sensors and can't help with this requirement. I did not invent efficiency numbers.

What I can offer is physics reasoning, and none of it comes from the documents:
- **Trapping in planar sensors:** at 2e16 neq/cm² the charge collection distance in planar silicon is roughly 10–30 µm. T3 (planar) would probably need a thin sensor, around 50–100 µm, to have a chance at 97%. T1 is probably planar-like too, so the same applies.
- **T1 charge sharing:** T1 spreads an already small signal over several pixels, so it is at risk against the threshold after irradiation.
- **T2 (3D):** the electrode spacing doesn't depend on thickness, so T2 is the most plausible technology to meet 97% at end of life. It also has the worst resolution, 14 µm at 150 µm unirradiated.

The gaps that block a verified answer are irradiated efficiency versus thickness for each technology, the chip threshold, the bias voltage limit, and the per-technology thickness ranges. Resolution versus thickness is also unknown beyond the single 150 µm point.

Any recommendation depends on external irradiated-efficiency data. If none can be found, T2 is the only defensible choice for the hard requirement, and it would have to be flagged as unverified. I recorded the gaps and this reasoning with `record_results`.
Step s2 produced no verified feasible set, so I'm running all three technologies across the thickness range. That covers the feasible candidates and the sanity-check points in one pass.
Optima look to be near 100–150 µm for T1, about 150 µm for T2 and 150–200 µm for T3. I'm adding finer steps around those.

content.text:
I ran the simulation for all three technologies from 50 to 300 µm and recorded every value with `record_results`. I ran all three because s2 left no verified feasible set, so no point could be labelled infeasible. The simulation is unirradiated only, so none of these numbers shows whether a sensor meets 97% efficiency at 2e16 neq/cm².

Single-hit resolution (µm, unirradiated):

| Thickness (µm) | T1 | T3 | T2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | 6.90 | 10.20 | 17.07 |
| 75 | 6.52 | 9.73 | – |
| 100 | 6.20 | 9.35 | 15.34 |
| 125 | 6.09 | 9.34 | 13.02 |
| 150 | 6.20 | 8.98 | 13.85 |
| 175 | – | 9.06 | 13.55 |
| 200 | 6.36 | 8.94 | 14.52 |
| 300 | 7.86 | 12.49 | 18.39 |

- **Ranking:** T1 is best at every thickness, then T3, then T2.
- **T1 optimum:** The best value is 6.09 µm at 125 µm. The curve is flat from 100 to 150 µm, with 6.2 µm at both ends.
- **T3 optimum:** The curve is flat at about 8.9–9.1 µm from 150 to 200 µm.
- **T2 optimum:** The best value is 13.0 µm at 125 µm. The T2 curve is noisy, since 125 µm comes out better than 150 µm.
- **Thin sensors:** All three technologies get worse at 50 µm, and T1 loses less than the others. For T1, going from 125 to 100 µm costs only about 0.1 µm. Thinner sensors are generally expected to hold up better after irradiation, so that small cost may be worth paying.
- **Noise:** The scatter between neighbouring points is roughly 0.3–0.5 µm, so the minima are broad.

The final recommendation will need to flag that efficiency at end of life is unverified.

**Recommendation (efficiency unverified): Sensor-T2 at 125 µm. The runner-up is Sensor-T1 at 100 µm.**

I could not check the 97% efficiency requirement at 2e16 neq/cm² for any technology. I re-read the project documents, and none has efficiency-versus-fluence data. None has an irradiated-resolution correction either, so I applied no correction.

- **Why T2:** I picked it from physics reasoning, not from data. A 3D sensor's electrode spacing doesn't depend on thickness, so it is the most likely to keep 97% efficiency after irradiation. T2's simulated unirradiated resolution at 125 µm is 13.0 µm.
- **What it costs:** T1 has the best simulated resolution at every thickness, at 6.1 µm at 125 µm. That is about 7 µm better than T2.
- **Runner-up:** T1 at 100 µm gives 6.2 µm unirradiated. It is only about 0.1 µm worse than T1 at 125 µm, and a thinner sensor should hold up better after irradiation. If external data show T1 reaches 97% at 2e16, it becomes the better choice.
- **Thickness sensitivity:**
  - T2 resolution is 15.3 µm at 100 µm, 17.1 µm at 50 µm and 18.4 µm at 300 µm.
  - The scatter between neighbouring T2 points is about 0.5–1 µm, so the 125 µm minimum is not sharp.
  - The T1 curve is flat from 100 to 150 µm.
- **Efficiency margin:** unknown.
- **Irradiated resolution:** the degradation is not quantified. It is likely to be worse for T1 because of its charge sharing and the readout threshold, and for thick planar sensors because of trapping.
